household.method_note: Illustrative tracker mortgage at Bank Rate plus 1pp. Most UK borrowers are on fixed rates and feel a change at remortgage (review H3).

levers.method_note: OBR ready reckoner: a 1 point rise in short-term interest rates adds 6.73bn to debt interest in 2026-27 and 5.04bn in 2030-31 (EFO-2026-03). Gilt yields are held fixed. Low–high is an editorial ±20%.

levers.label: VAT standard rate

cpi_provenance.method_note: One-off rise in the CPI level per 1 point on the standard rate of VAT. The Bank of England estimated that the January 2011 rise from 17.5% to 20% added 0.7, about 1 and 1.4 percentage points to CPI inflation if half, three quarters (its central case) or all of it reached prices; divided by the 2.5-point rise, that is 0.28 (low), 0.40 (central) and 0.56 (high). VAT applies to around two thirds of the CPI basket. The ONS measured about 0.76 points for the same rise (0.30 per point) in the month it took effect. The effect drops out of annual inflation after about 12 months.

levers.method_note: HMRC direct effect of 1 point on the standard rate of VAT: 8.8bn in 2026-27, 9.55bn by 2028-29 (HMRC-DE-2025-06). Low–high is an editorial ±10% because HMRC publishes a central figure only. HMRC includes taxpayers' own behavioural response where it models one, but no wider economic effects.

levers.label: Corporation tax main rate
levers.method_note: HMRC direct effect of 1 point on the main rate of corporation tax: 3.6bn in 2026-27, 4bn by 2028-29 (HMRC-DE-2025-06). Low–high is an editorial ±10% because HMRC publishes a central figure only. HMRC includes taxpayers' own behavioural response where it models one, but no wider economic effects.

HMRC direct effect of 1p a litre on the main rate of fuel duty: 0.414bn in 2026-27, 0.397bn by 2028-29 (HMRC-DE-2025-06). Low–high is an editorial ±10% because HMRC publishes a central figure only. HMRC includes taxpayers' own behavioural response where it models one, but no wider economic effects. Derived, not published: HMRC's 1% petrol + diesel rows (240m) divided by 1% of a 57.95p/litre main rate, so 1p/litre = 1% x 100/57.95. 57.95p is the bulletin's current rate plus the pence its notes say the baseline adds back. HMRC also uprates the baseline rate by forecast RPI each April, so this overstates 1p by roughly cumulative RPI (a few % in year one, more later). Includes behavioural response; no economy-wide effects. Starting rate 52.95p a litre, in force since 2022-03-23 (GOV.UK). Already scheduled: 55.95p from 2027-01-01; 57.95p from 2027-03-01.
levers.label: Fuel duty, main rate

levers.method_note: HMRC's estimates for raising the lower rate of capital gains tax, with the change made at the start of 2026-27 (HMRC-DE-2025-06). +1 point: −£5m in 2026-27, +£5m in 2028-29; +5 points: −£40m in 2026-27, −£10m in 2028-29; +10 points: −£130m in 2026-27, −£135m in 2028-29. A minus means the Treasury collects less: HMRC's figures allow for people selling fewer assets when the rate rises. These are HMRC's only steps (+1, +5, +10 points), so the sandbox offers no others and never scales or blends them: HMRC says its capital gains tax figures “are also non-linear and so cannot be scaled up”. Taxing these gains at the basic rate of income tax (20% in England, Wales and Northern Ireland) would need a rise of 2 points, which is not one of HMRC's steps. Starting rate 18%, the rate for 2026-27 (GOV.UK). Low–high is an editorial ±10% because HMRC publishes a central figure only. HMRC includes taxpayers' own behavioural response where it models one, but no wider economic effects.
levers.label: Capital gains tax, lower rate

levers.method_note: HMRC's estimates for raising the higher rate of capital gains tax, with the change made at the start of 2026-27 (HMRC-DE-2025-06). +1 point: −£15m in 2026-27, −£30m in 2028-29; +5 points: −£170m in 2026-27, −£870m in 2028-29; +10 points: −£540m in 2026-27, −£3,565m in 2028-29. A minus means the Treasury collects less: HMRC's figures allow for people selling fewer assets when the rate rises. These are HMRC's only steps (+1, +5, +10 points), so the sandbox offers no others and never scales or blends them: HMRC says its capital gains tax figures “are also non-linear and so cannot be scaled up”. Taxing these gains at the higher rate of income tax (40% in England, Wales and Northern Ireland) would need a rise of 16 points, bigger than any HMRC estimates. Starting rate 24%, the rate for 2026-27 (GOV.UK). Low–high is an editorial ±10% because HMRC publishes a central figure only. HMRC includes taxpayers' own behavioural response where it models one, but no wider economic effects.
levers.label: Capital gains tax, higher rate
Defence, % of GDP (NATO measure)
levers.method_note: Starting point: UK defence spending on NATO's definition, 2.32% of GDP in 2025-26 (a NATO estimate), NATO-DE-2026-07. NATO counts more items than the UK's own COFOG figure (65.4bn, 2.13% of GDP). Each point of GDP is 30.7bn (2025-26 nominal GDP, as in the Statement), added to defence spending.

HMRC also uprates the baseline rate by forecast RPI each April, so this overstates 1p by roughly cumulative RPI (a few % in year one, more later). macro_rules.method_note: OBR first-year fiscal multipliers: a change worth 1% of GDP moves real GDP by 0.45% for day-to-day public services, 0.6% for welfare and 1% for investment (October 2024 EFO, FOI table 1.1), so spending runs from 0.45 (low) through 0.6 (central) to 1.0 (high). Tax: 0.33 in the OBR's current single multiplier (central), and 0.3 for income tax and National Insurance and 0.35 for VAT in its earlier published framework (low and high; OBR fiscal multipliers box). The sandbox applies one spending and one tax multiplier to every lever, so the result is an approximation; the OBR also tapers multipliers to zero over five years. Year-1 GDP effect = (spending multiplier × Δ non-interest spending − tax multiplier × Δ tax) / GDP.
